The corpus contains the EMA Reflection Paper on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Lifecycle of Medicines (EMA/CHMP/CVMP/83833/2023), which is a final reflection paper adopted by CHMP on 9 September 2024 and by CVMP on 11 September 2024 [16]. The corpus also contains EU GMP Annex 22 on Artificial Intelligence, which is identified as a draft consultation document [3]. As a draft, the Annex 22 provisions represent proposals under consultation and do not yet constitute binding requirements; they should be read in conditional terms.

Taken together, these two documents address the ethical and quality governance framework for AI in pharmacovigilance signal detection across complementary dimensions.

On the ethical governance side, the Reflection Paper establishes that the basic ethical principles for trustworthy AI — encompassing human agency and oversight, technical robustness and safety, privacy and data governance, transparency, accountability, societal and environmental well-being, and diversity, non-discrimination and fairness — apply across all phases of the medicinal product lifecycle for human medicines and, to an appropriate degree, for veterinary medicines [14]. These principles, derived from the European Commission's High-Level Expert Group on AI and its Assessment List for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (ALTAI), are presented as the normative foundation for all AI/ML deployment, including pharmacovigilance applications [14]. The Reflection Paper requires a systematic impact analysis to be conducted in the early stages of planning and development, with expertise on ethical and legal aspects, including data protection for privacy by design, onboarded early in all projects [14].

With respect to pharmacovigilance specifically, the Reflection Paper acknowledges that applications within pharmacovigilance may allow a more flexible approach to AI/ML modelling and deployment, where incremental learning can continuously enhance models for classification and severity scoring of adverse event reports as well as signal detection [15]. However, it unambiguously places responsibility on the marketing authorisation holder: it remains the responsibility of the MAH to validate, monitor and document model performance and to include AI/ML operations in the pharmacovigilance system, in order to mitigate risks related to all algorithms and models used [15]. Where a post-authorisation study is listed as a condition of a marketing authorisation, AI/ML applications should be discussed within a regulatory procedure unless details were agreed at the time of authorisation, and the same requirements applicable to pivotal clinical trials — including a pre-specified statistical analysis plan, data pipeline and frozen models — may apply [15].

On the quality and procedural governance side, the Reflection Paper requires that SOPs implementing GxP principles on data and algorithm governance be extended to cover all data, models and algorithms used for AI/ML in cases of high regulatory impact or high patient risk, and that governance of all components, data protection compliance and adherence to ethical standards be documented and regularly reviewed [21].

The draft EU GMP Annex 22 contributes specific technical quality controls that are proposed to apply to AI models used for prediction or classification, which would encompass signal detection models. The draft proposes that systems should, where applicable, log the confidence score of the model for each prediction or classification outcome [3]. It further proposes that models used to predict or classify data should have an appropriate threshold setting to ensure predictions or classifications are made only when suitable, and that where the confidence score is very low, consideration should be given to whether the model should flag the outcome as 'undecided' rather than making potentially unreliable predictions or classifications [3]. These provisions, if finalised, would operationalise the robustness and transparency principles articulated in the Reflection Paper by translating them into concrete output-level controls.

On the question of test data quality, the draft Annex 22 proposes that test data be representative of and expand the full sample space of the intended use, stratified to include all subgroups and reflect the limitations, complexity and all common and rare variations within the intended use [4]. Test datasets and their subgroups should be sufficient in size to calculate test metrics with adequate statistical confidence, labelling should be verified to a very high degree of correctness, and generation of test data or labels by means of generative AI is not recommended [4]. These provisions directly support the Reflection Paper's emphasis on minimising bias and ensuring fairness, including in subgroup representation — concerns that are particularly material in pharmacovigilance signal detection where under-represented populations may carry differential risk profiles.

In summary, the Reflection Paper provides the overarching ethical framework, assigns MAH responsibility for lifecycle governance of AI in pharmacovigilance, and connects to GxP documentation and regulatory interaction obligations, while the draft GMP Annex 22 proposes to complement this with granular quality system requirements for model output confidence, threshold management and test data integrity. The latter's requirements remain subject to finalisation and should not yet be treated as binding obligations.

results.question_text: We are building our computerised system register to satisfy Annex 11. What does Annex 11 require the register to contain, and how should ICH Q10 change management requirements inform what additional system knowledge we document?

EU GMP Annex 11 requires that an up-to-date listing of all relevant systems and their GMP functionality — commonly referred to as an inventory — should be available [12]. For critical systems specifically, this inventory requirement is augmented: an up-to-date system description detailing the physical and logical arrangements, data flows and interfaces with other systems or processes, any hardware and software prerequisites, and security measures should also be available [12].

Beyond the inventory itself, Annex 11 establishes several categories of information that, taken together, define what a well-maintained system register must be capable of supporting. Validation documentation and reports should cover the relevant steps of the lifecycle, with manufacturers able to justify their standards, protocols, acceptance criteria, procedures and records based on risk assessment [21]. Validation documentation should include change control records (if applicable) and reports on any deviations observed during the validation process [17]. User Requirements Specifications should describe the required functions of the computerised system and be based on documented risk assessment and GMP impact, with user requirements remaining traceable throughout the lifecycle [20]. For critical systems, evidence of appropriate test methods and test scenarios should be demonstrated, with particular attention to system parameter limits, data limits and error handling [11]. Where data are transferred to another data format or system, validation should include checks that data are not altered in value or meaning during the migration process [19].

Risk management should be applied throughout the lifecycle of the computerised system, taking into account patient safety, data integrity and product quality, and decisions on the extent of validation and data integrity controls should be based on a justified and documented risk assessment [26]. Periodic evaluation is also required to confirm that systems remain in a valid state and are compliant with GMP; such evaluations should include, where appropriate, the current range of functionality, deviation records, incidents, problems, upgrade history, performance, reliability, security and validation status reports [3]. Any changes to a computerised system including system configurations should only be made in a controlled manner in accordance with a defined procedure [18].

Turning to how ICH Q10 change management principles should inform what additional system knowledge is documented: ICH Q10 describes a systematic approach to proposing, evaluating, approving, implementing and reviewing changes as a core element of the pharmaceutical quality system [9]. ICH Q10 augments GMP requirements by describing specific quality system elements and management responsibilities, and encourages the use of science- and risk-based approaches at each lifecycle stage to promote continual improvement [1]. Knowledge management and quality risk management are identified as enablers that facilitate science- and risk-based decisions related to product quality [2].

Applied to a computerised system register, this ICH Q10 framework means that the register should capture not merely the current validated state of a system but the knowledge generated across its entire lifecycle — including the rationale for change decisions, the risk assessments that underpinned those decisions, and the outcome of post-change evaluations. Where Annex 11 requires change control records within validation documentation [17] and mandates that changes be made in a controlled manner [18], ICH Q10 provides the quality system architecture within which that controlled process should operate: changes should be proposed, evaluated against documented risk assessments, approved by appropriately qualified personnel, implemented, and then reviewed to confirm the intended outcome was achieved.

In practical terms, the system register should therefore document, for each system: the current GMP functionality classification and criticality determination; the validated state including the lifecycle documentation referenced in Annex 11 §4; a complete and current change history cross-referenced to the change control records required under Annex 11 §4.2; the outcomes of periodic evaluations conducted under Annex 11 §11; incident and deviation records as required under Annex 11 §13; and the risk assessment basis for all validation scope and data integrity control decisions under Annex 11 §1. The ICH Q10 principle of knowledge management reinforces that this documented system knowledge should be maintained in a manner that is accessible and useful for future change proposals and continual improvement activities, rather than treated as static archival records [2].

results.question_text: What requirements do 21 CFR Part 11 and the FDA data integrity guidance together impose on the design of a system where paper printouts are used as original records alongside the electronic system?
results.expected_answer_scope: Must combine FDA DI Q&A section on static vs dynamic records and paper printout retention with 21 CFR Part 11 §11.2 on using electronic records in lieu of paper, clarifying when each applies.
results.answer:
The FDA data integrity guidance and 21 CFR Part 11 together impose a layered set of requirements on systems where paper printouts are used alongside an electronic system. The applicable requirements depend on whether the paper printout constitutes a genuine original record or whether the electronic record is the original record of which the paper is merely a copy.

On the question of when a paper printout may serve as the original record, the FDA data integrity guidance distinguishes between static and dynamic records. A static record is a fixed-data record such as a paper record or an electronic image, while a dynamic record format allows interaction between the user and the record content, for example permitting a user to change the baseline and reprocess chromatographic data so that resulting peaks may appear smaller or larger [25]. A paper printout or static record may satisfy retention requirements only if it is the original record or a true copy of the original record [18]. During data acquisition, for example, pH meters and balances may create a paper printout or static record as the original record, and in that case the paper printout, or a true copy, must be retained [18].

However, where laboratory instruments generate dynamic electronic records, a printout or static record does not preserve the dynamic record format that is part of the complete original record [18]. The guidance uses FT-IR spectroscopy as an example: the spectral file is dynamic and can be reprocessed, and a static record or printout would not satisfy the CGMP requirements to retain original records or true copies under § 211.180(d) [18]. Furthermore, if the full spectrum is not displayed in the printout, contaminants may be excluded, which compounds the integrity concern [18].

Where electronic records exist, the system design must ensure that changes to computerised records can be made only by authorised personnel under § 211.68(b) [11]. The system administrator role, including any rights to alter files and settings, should be assigned to personnel independent from those responsible for the record content, and manufacturers must establish and implement a method for documenting authorised personnel's access privileges for each CGMP computer system [11]. Login credentials must not be shared, because when they are, a unique individual cannot be identified through the login and the system would not conform to CGMP requirements in Parts 211 and 212 [14].

Audit trail requirements attach to the electronic system regardless of whether paper printouts are also maintained. Audit trails track creation, modification, or deletion of data such as processing parameters and results, as well as actions at the record or system level such as attempts to access the system or rename or delete a file [31]. Personnel responsible for record review under CGMP must review the audit trails that capture changes to data associated with the record as they review the rest of the record [21]. All production and control records, which include audit trails, must be reviewed and approved by the quality unit under § 211.192 [21].

The electronic records must also be accompanied by all associated metadata. Metadata is the contextual information required to understand data, and may include a date/time stamp, a user ID of the person who conducted the test or analysis, the instrument ID used to acquire the data, and audit trails [9]. Data must be maintained throughout the record's retention period with all associated metadata required to reconstruct the CGMP activity, and the relationships between data and their metadata must be preserved in a secure and traceable manner [9].

With respect to true copies, electronic copies can be used as true copies of paper or electronic records provided the copies preserve the content and meaning of the original record, which includes all metadata required to reconstruct the CGMP activity, and the static or dynamic nature of the original records [37]. results.question_text: We are investigating a data integrity deviation where an analyst was found to have deleted and re-entered out-of-trend HPLC results. What do ICH Q10 CAPA requirements and the FDA data integrity Q&A guidance together require us to document and implement before we can close this investigation?

This question requires synthesising requirements from two sources: the FDA Data Integrity and Compliance With Drug CGMP Q&A guidance (December 2018) and ICH Q10. The following sets out what each framework requires, and how they interact in the context of this specific deviation.

**Nature of the Violation and Mandatory Investigation**

The deletion and re-entry of out-of-trend HPLC results constitutes suspected falsification or alteration of CGMP records. Regardless of intent or how or from whom the information was received, suspected or known falsification or alteration of records required under parts 210, 211, and 212 must be fully investigated under the CGMP quality system to determine the effect of the event on patient safety, product quality, and data reliability, to determine the root cause, and to ensure the necessary corrective actions are taken [33]. All data — including obvious errors and failing, passing, and suspect data — must be in the CGMP records that are retained and subject to review and oversight, and an investigation with documented, scientifically sound justification is necessary for any data to be invalidated and not used in determining conformance to specification for a batch [30].

FDA data integrity guidance defines data integrity as the completeness, consistency, and accuracy of data, where complete, consistent, and accurate data should be attributable, legible, contemporaneously recorded, original or a true copy, and accurate (ALCOA), and states that data integrity is critical throughout the CGMP data life cycle including in the creation, modification, processing, maintenance, archival, retrieval, transmission, and disposition of data [32]. The act of deleting and re-entering results directly violates the ALCOA principles, particularly the requirements for original records and contemporaneous recording.

**Audit Trail and Record Completeness Requirements**

Audit trails include those that track creation, modification, or deletion of data such as processing parameters and results, as well as those that track actions at the record or system level such as attempts to access the system or rename or delete a file [34]. Personnel responsible for record review under CGMP should review the audit trails that capture changes to data associated with the record as they review the rest of the record, and all production and control records, which includes audit trails, must be reviewed and approved by the quality unit [24]. Your investigation documentation must therefore include a complete audit trail review demonstrating the full scope of the deletions and re-entries, and the quality unit must formally review and approve the findings.

Metadata — including date/time stamps, user IDs, and instrument IDs — must be maintained throughout the record's retention period with all associated metadata required to reconstruct the CGMP activity, and the relationships between data and their metadata should be preserved in a secure and traceable manner [12]. The investigation record must reconstruct, to the extent possible, the original deleted data using audit trail metadata.

Electronic records from laboratory instruments such as HPLC systems are dynamic, and a printout or static record does not preserve the dynamic record format that is part of the complete original record [21]. This means that the investigation must address whether the underlying dynamic electronic records — not merely printouts — have been preserved, and whether the deletion has compromised the ability to reconstruct the original chromatographic data.

**Access Controls and System Deficiencies**

The investigation must also address how the deletion was technically possible. FDA requires that changes to computerised CGMP records or input of laboratory data into computerised records can be made only by authorised personnel, and recommends restricting the ability to alter specifications, process parameters, data, or manufacturing or testing methods by technical means where possible [14]. The system administrator role, including any rights to alter files and settings, should be assigned to personnel independent from those responsible for the record content [14]. Your CAPA must therefore evaluate and document whether access controls were inadequate, whether the analyst had permissions that should not have been available, and implement technical remediation accordingly.

**ICH Q10 CAPA Requirements**

Under ICH Q10, the pharmaceutical company should have a system for implementing corrective actions and preventive actions resulting from the investigation of non-conformances and findings, and a structured approach to the investigation process should be used with the objective of determining the root cause [4]. The level of effort, formality, and documentation of the investigation should be commensurate with the level of risk, in line with ICH Q9, and CAPA methodology should result in product and process improvements and enhanced product and process understanding [4]. For commercial manufacturing specifically, CAPA should be used and the effectiveness of the actions should be evaluated [4].

This means the investigation file must document: the root cause determination (whether systemic, individual, or both); the impact assessment on product quality and patient safety; the specific corrective actions taken; the preventive actions designed to prevent recurrence; and a defined mechanism to evaluate the effectiveness of those actions after implementation. A CAPA that closes without an effectiveness check would not satisfy ICH Q10's requirement that effectiveness be evaluated in the commercial manufacturing context [4].

**Personnel and Training**

Training personnel to prevent and detect data integrity issues is consistent with the personnel requirements under sections 211.25 and 212.10, which require that personnel have the education, training, and experience to perform their assigned duties [2]. Your CAPA must therefore include documented retraining — not only for the analyst involved, but across the relevant population where a systemic gap is identified — and evidence that training addresses both the prohibition on data manipulation and the detection of such behaviour.

**Remediation and Management Strategy**

Where data integrity issues are identified, FDA expects the firm to investigate to determine the problem's scope and root causes, conduct a scientifically sound risk assessment of its potential effects including impact on data used to support submissions, and implement a management strategy including a global corrective action plan that addresses the root causes [29][23]. This may include retaining a third-party auditor and removing individuals responsible for data integrity lapses from positions where they can influence CGMP-related or drug application data, as well as improvements in quality oversight, enhanced computer systems, and creation of mechanisms to prevent recurrences [23].

**Summary of Documentation Required to Close the Investigation**

Taken together, the investigation file must contain: a complete audit trail review with the quality unit's formal approval; a reconstructed record of the original deleted data to the extent technically possible; a documented root cause determination; a risk assessment of impact on product quality, patient safety, and any regulatory submissions; corrective actions addressing the specific act of deletion and re-entry; preventive actions addressing systemic access control and oversight failures; enhanced technical controls restricting data alteration by analysts; documented retraining of relevant personnel; a defined CAPA effectiveness check with a timeline; and, where the scope of the issue extends beyond a single event, evidence of a broader data governance review. Any data that cannot be reconstructed or verified must be treated as unreliable, and the impact on batch disposition and any prior regulatory submissions must be documented and addressed.

results.question_text: We are implementing a new MES that will generate electronic batch records as the primary GMP record, replacing paper. What do EU GMP Annex 11, 21 CFR Part 11, and ICH Q10 together require us to address in the validation plan, change management documentation, and quality system procedures before go-live?
results.expected_answer_scope: A correct answer must integrate Annex 11 validation and audit trail requirements, 21 CFR Part 11 electronic record and signature controls, and ICH Q10 change management and knowledge management obligations that collectively govern the transition from paper to electronic batch records.
results.answer:
This question spans three regulatory frameworks that together establish a comprehensive set of requirements for implementing a Manufacturing Execution System (MES) generating electronic batch records as the primary GMP record. The following addresses each area in turn, drawing on all three frameworks.

VALIDATION PLAN

Under EU GMP Annex 11, the application must be validated and the IT infrastructure qualified before go-live [57]. Risk management must be applied throughout the lifecycle of the computerised system, taking into account patient safety, data integrity, and product quality, and decisions on the extent of validation and data integrity controls must be based on a justified and documented risk assessment [46]. Validation documentation and reports must cover the relevant steps of the life cycle, and manufacturers must be able to justify their standards, protocols, acceptance criteria, procedures, and records based on their risk assessment [41]. User Requirements Specifications must describe the required functions of the computerised system, be based on documented risk assessment and GMP impact, and user requirements must be traceable throughout the lifecycle [40]. For critical systems, an up-to-date system description detailing physical and logical arrangements, data flows, interfaces with other systems or processes, hardware and software prerequisites, and security measures must be available [32]. Evidence of appropriate test methods and test scenarios must be demonstrated, and system parameter limits, data limits, and error handling must be considered; automated testing tools and test environments must have documented assessments for their adequacy [31]. Where data are transferred to another data format or system, validation must include checks that data are not altered in value or meaning during the migration process [39]. Regular backups of all relevant data must be performed, and integrity, accuracy of backup data, and the ability to restore data must be checked during validation and monitored periodically [55].

Under 21 CFR Part 11, persons using closed systems to create, modify, maintain, or transmit electronic records must employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity, and, when appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records [17]. Specifically, systems must be validated to ensure accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance, and the ability to discern invalid or altered records [17]. The system must have the ability to generate accurate and complete copies of records in both human-readable and electronic form suitable for inspection, review, and copying by the agency [17]. Computer systems, controls, and attendant documentation maintained under Part 11 must be readily available for, and subject to, FDA inspection [25].

CHANGE MANAGEMENT DOCUMENTATION

Under EU GMP Annex 11, any changes to a computerised system including system configurations must only be made in a controlled manner in accordance with a defined procedure [38]. Validation documentation must include change control records where applicable, and reports on any deviations observed during the validation process [37]. Computerised systems must be periodically evaluated to confirm that they remain in a valid state and are compliant with GMP, and such evaluations must include, where appropriate, the current range of functionality, deviation records, incidents, problems, upgrade history, performance, reliability, security, and validation status reports [5]. Where relevant changes are to be made to the system after go-live, the ability to retrieve archived data must be ensured and tested [59].

Under 21 CFR Part 11, revision and change control procedures must be maintained to maintain an audit trail that documents time-sequenced development and modification of systems documentation [19]. Adequate controls over the distribution of, access to, and use of documentation for system operation and maintenance must also be in place [19].

Under ICH Q10, the quality system elements and management responsibilities described in the guideline are intended to encourage the use of science and risk-based approaches at each lifecycle stage, thereby promoting continual improvement across the entire product lifecycle [3]. ICH Q10 augments GMPs by describing specific quality system elements and management responsibilities, and is intended to be used together with regional GMP requirements [3]. Consequently, change management procedures for the MES must be embedded within the broader Pharmaceutical Quality System framework to ensure that changes are assessed for their impact on product quality and process control across the product lifecycle [4].

QUALITY SYSTEM PROCEDURES BEFORE GO-LIVE

On access controls and electronic signatures, EU GMP Annex 11 requires that physical and logical controls be in place to restrict access to authorised persons, that creation, change, and cancellation of access authorisations be recorded, and that management systems for data and documents be designed to record the identity of operators entering, changing, confirming, or deleting data including date and time [56]. When the MES is used for recording certification and batch release, the system must allow only Qualified Persons to certify the release of batches, must clearly identify and record the person releasing or certifying batches, and this must be performed using an electronic signature [52]. Under 21 CFR Part 11, each electronic signature must be unique to one individual and must not be reused by or reassigned to anyone else, and the identity of each individual must be verified before an electronic signature is established [26]. Non-biometric electronic signatures must employ at least two distinct identification components such as an identification code and password [20]. Persons using electronic signatures must, prior to or at the time of such use, certify to the FDA that the electronic signatures in their system are intended to be the legally binding equivalent of traditional handwritten signatures [26]. Signed electronic records must contain the printed name of the signer, the date and time when the signature was executed, and the meaning associated with the signature, and these items must be included as part of any human-readable form of the electronic record [29].

On audit trails, 21 CFR Part 11 requires the use of secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails to independently record the date and time of operator entries and actions that create, modify, or delete electronic records; record changes must not obscure previously recorded information; and audit trail documentation must be retained for a period at least as long as that required for the subject electronic records and must be available for agency review and copying [14]. EU GMP Annex 11 requires that, based on a risk assessment, the system create a record of all GMP-relevant changes and deletions, that the reason for change or deletion of GMP-relevant data be documented, and that audit trails be available, convertible to a generally intelligible form, and regularly reviewed [53]. For records supporting batch release, it must be possible to generate printouts indicating if any of the data has been changed since the original entry [48].

On data integrity and backup, data must be secured by both physical and electronic means against damage, stored data must be checked for accessibility, readability, and accuracy, and access to data must be ensured throughout the retention period [36]. It must be possible to obtain clear printed copies of electronically stored data [48].

On personnel and third-party suppliers, there must be close cooperation between all relevant personnel including the Process Owner, System Owner, Qualified Persons, and IT, and all personnel must have appropriate qualifications, level of access, and defined responsibilities [35]. Persons who develop, maintain, or use electronic record and electronic signature systems must have the education, training, and experience to perform their assigned tasks [19]. Where third parties are involved in providing, installing, configuring, integrating, or validating the MES, formal agreements must exist with clear statements of the responsibilities of the third party, and IT departments must be considered analogous to third parties [43]. The competence and reliability of the supplier must be assessed, and the need for an audit must be based on a risk assessment [45]. Quality system and audit information relating to suppliers or developers must be made available to inspectors on request [47].

On business continuity, for computerised systems supporting critical processes, provisions must be made to ensure continuity of support for those processes in the event of a system breakdown, including a manual or alternative system; the time required to bring alternative arrangements into use must be based on risk and appropriate for the particular system and business process it supports; and these arrangements must be adequately documented and tested [34].

On electronic records in lieu of paper, under 21 CFR Part 11, for records required to be maintained but not submitted to the agency, persons may use electronic records in lieu of paper records or electronic signatures in lieu of traditional signatures provided that the requirements of Part 11 are met [16]. Electronic records meeting the requirements of Part 11 may be used in lieu of paper records in accordance with § 11.2, unless paper records are specifically required [25]. Additionally, EU GMP Annex 15 confirms that computerised systems used for the manufacture of medicinal products must also be validated according to the requirements of Annex 11, and that the relevant concepts and guidance presented in ICH Q8, Q9, Q10, and Q11 must be taken into account [9].

Taken together, these frameworks require that the validation plan be risk-based and lifecycle-spanning, that change management be procedurally controlled with documented audit trails, and that the quality system integrate access controls, electronic signature certification, data integrity controls, personnel qualification, supplier management, and business continuity provisions before the MES goes live as the primary GMP record system.

results.question_text: Our QMS SOP for supplier qualification currently covers approved supplier lists and audits. How do ICH Q10 requirements for oversight of outsourced activities and the FDA data integrity Q&A guidance together require us to extend this SOP to cover data integrity risks at contract laboratories?
results.expected_answer_scope: A correct answer must specify ICH Q10 requirements for quality agreements and outsourced activity oversight combined with FDA DI guidance expectations for verifying contractor data integrity controls, audit trail availability, and raw data access during audits.

The two source documents together establish a layered framework that, when read in combination, requires your supplier qualification SOP to extend materially beyond approved supplier lists and audits to address data integrity risks at contract laboratories specifically.

ICH Q10 §2.7 establishes that the pharmaceutical company is ultimately responsible for ensuring that processes are in place to assure the control of outsourced activities and the quality of purchased materials, and that these processes should incorporate quality risk management [3]. The specific obligations under ICH Q10 include assessing the suitability and competence of the contract acceptor prior to outsourcing operations using a defined supply chain, including through audits and qualification activities [3]. Critically, the framework requires that the responsibilities and communication processes for quality-related activities be defined in a written agreement between the contract giver and contract acceptor [3]. ICH Q10 further requires ongoing monitoring and review of the performance of the contract acceptor and the identification and implementation of any needed improvements [3]. Each of these obligations has a direct data integrity dimension when the outsourced activity involves the generation, processing, or retention of CGMP data.

The FDA Data Integrity Q&A guidance establishes the substantive data integrity requirements that must flow through those ICH Q10 governance mechanisms. Data integrity is defined as the completeness, consistency, and accuracy of data, and complete, consistent, and accurate data must be attributable, legible, contemporaneously recorded, original or a true copy, and accurate — the ALCOA standard — throughout the entire CGMP data life cycle, including creation, modification, processing, maintenance, archival, retrieval, transmission, and disposition [26]. These requirements apply equally to data generated at contract laboratories, because all records required under CGMP are subject to FDA inspection regardless of where they are generated, and this applies to records maintained on computerized systems including electronic communications that support CGMP activities [30].

The written quality agreement required by ICH Q10 §2.7(b) must therefore define data integrity responsibilities with precision [3]. The FDA guidance specifies that system controls, including documentation controls, must be designed in accordance with CGMP to assure product quality, and that actions must be attributable to a specific individual, which precludes shared login credentials [11]. Access to computerized CGMP records must be restricted to authorized personnel, and the system administrator role must be assigned to personnel independent from those responsible for record content [8]. Your SOP and the quality agreement it governs should specify these requirements as contractual obligations on the contract laboratory.

Audit trail requirements are particularly significant for contract laboratory oversight. The FDA guidance defines an audit trail as a secure, computer-generated, time-stamped electronic record that allows for reconstruction of the course of events relating to the creation, modification, or deletion of an electronic record, and provides as an example that the audit trail for an HPLC run should include the user name, date/time of the run, integration parameters used, and details of any reprocessing [41]. Audit trail review is expressly required as part of CGMP record review, with the review frequency determined either by specific regulatory requirements or by a risk assessment evaluating data criticality, control mechanisms, and impact on product quality [35]. Your SOP should extend this risk-based audit trail review obligation to cover data generated by contract laboratories, consistent with the ICH Q10 requirement to monitor and review contract acceptor performance on an ongoing basis [3].

Testing into compliance is a specific data integrity risk that is directly relevant to contract laboratory oversight. FDA prohibits sampling and testing with the goal of achieving a specific result, and considers it a violative practice to use actual samples in test, prep, or equilibration runs as a means of disguising testing into compliance [7]. All data, including obvious errors and failing, passing, and suspect data, must be in the CGMP records that are retained and subject to review and oversight, and invalidation of data requires a documented, scientifically sound justification [24]. Your SOP should establish mechanisms — such as audit trail review, data governance provisions in the quality agreement, and periodic audits — that specifically assess whether contract laboratories are generating and retaining complete datasets and not selectively reporting results.

The FDA guidance also requires that electronic records from dynamic laboratory instruments be retained in their dynamic format rather than as static printouts, because a static record or printout does not preserve the dynamic record format that is part of the complete original record [15]. Backup data must be exact, complete, and secure from alteration, inadvertent erasures, or loss, and must be maintained in the original format or a format compatible with the original format [33]. Your SOP should require that quality agreements specify the format in which contract laboratory records must be maintained and transmitted to the contract giver, and that this format satisfies the FDA requirements for original records or true copies.

The FDA guidance also confirms that personnel must have the education, training, and experience to perform their assigned duties, and that training to prevent and detect data integrity issues is consistent with these requirements [2]. This training obligation extends logically, through the ICH Q10 monitoring and oversight framework, to verifying that contract laboratory personnel responsible for CGMP data generation and review have received adequate data integrity training — a matter that should be addressed in audit scope and quality agreement provisions within your SOP.

Taken together, these two instruments require your supplier qualification SOP to incorporate, at minimum: data integrity-specific criteria in the pre-qualification assessment of contract laboratories; quality agreement provisions that specify ALCOA data integrity obligations, audit trail requirements, access controls, data retention format requirements, and prohibitions on testing into compliance; a risk-based programme for ongoing audit trail review of contract laboratory data; and defined communication and escalation processes for data integrity deviations identified at contract facilities. Queries requiring legal interpretation of these requirements as they apply to specific contractual arrangements should be referred to a qualified regulatory professional.
